title: Explain time complexity and space complexity, with common Big-O examples.
shortTitle: Time complexity and space complexity, with common Big-O examples

s1_definition.profdef: Time complexity describes how the running time of an algorithm grows as the size of its input grows, and space complexity describes how the amount of extra memory it needs grows with input size. Both are expressed using Big-O notation, which captures the dominant growth rate while ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. Big-O gives an upper bound on growth, letting you compare algorithms independently of hardware, so you can predict how a solution behaves when the data goes from a thousand rows to ten million.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a ledger and you want to find Rajesh's account. If the ledger is a sorted index card box and you flip through every card one by one, the time grows directly with the number of customers — a million customers means up to a million flips. That is linear time. But if the cards are sorted and you use the phone-book trick of opening the middle and halving each time, a million customers take only about twenty checks. That is logarithmic time. Big-O is just a way of saying "as the bank grows to millions of customers, how much slower does this method get, and how much extra scratch paper do I need?"
s1_definition.oneliner: Time complexity is how running time scales with input size, space complexity is how extra memory scales, and Big-O names the growth rate ignoring constants.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Time complexity describes how the running time of an algorithm grows as the size of its input grows, and space complexity describes how the amount of extra memory it needs grows with input size. Both are expressed using Big-O notation, which captures the dominant growth rate while ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. Big-O gives an upper bound on growth, letting you compare algorithms independently of hardware, so you can predict how a solution behaves when the data goes from a thousand rows to ten million.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has a ledger and you want to find Rajesh's account. If the ledger is a sorted index card box and you flip through every card one by one, the time grows directly with the number of customers — a million customers means up to a million flips. That is linear time. But if the cards are sorted and you use the phone-book trick of opening the middle and halving each time, a million customers take only about twenty checks. That is logarithmic time. Big-O is just a way of saying "as the bank grows to millions of customers, how much slower does this method get, and how much extra scratch paper do I need?"

**One line to remember:** Time complexity is how running time scales with input size, space complexity is how extra memory scales, and Big-O names the growth rate ignoring constants.

sections.s2_technical:
Big-O focuses on the **dominant term** as input size n becomes large. If an algorithm does 3n plus 100 operations, we call it O(n), because for large n the 3 and the 100 do not matter compared to how n grows. We always drop constant multipliers and lower-order terms. We usually care about the **worst case**, though sometimes average case matters too.

Here are the common classes from fastest-growing-slowest to fastest-growing. **O(1), constant time**, means the work does not depend on input size at all. Looking up a value in a `HashMap` by key, or reading `array[5]`, is O(1). In banking, fetching Rajesh's cached balance by account id from a map is constant time no matter how many customers exist.

**O(log n), logarithmic time**, means the work grows very slowly, roughly by one step each time the input doubles. Binary search on a sorted array is O(log n). Finding an account in a balanced tree structure like a `TreeMap` is O(log n). A million entries take only about twenty comparisons.

**O(n), linear time**, means the work grows in direct proportion to input size. Scanning every transaction in a list once to sum the total is O(n). Iterating all accounts to find those below minimum balance is O(n).

**O(n log n)**, means doing linear work a logarithmic number of times. This is the complexity of good general-purpose sorting — `Collections.sort` and `Arrays.sort` for objects use a merge-sort variant that is O(n log n). Sorting a day's transactions by amount is O(n log n).

**O(n squared), quadratic time**, means the work grows with the square of the input, typically from a nested loop where each element is compared with every other. Comparing every transaction with every other transaction to find duplicates with a naive double loop is O(n squared). This becomes painfully slow quickly — ten thousand items means a hundred million operations.

**O(2 to the n), exponential**, and **O(n factorial)** are extremely expensive and appear in brute-force combinatorial problems, such as trying every subset or every ordering. These are impractical beyond tiny inputs and usually signal you need a smarter algorithm or dynamic programming.

**Space complexity** follows the same idea but counts extra memory, not time, and we usually exclude the input itself. An in-place algorithm that uses a fixed number of variables is O(1) space. Building a new list that copies all n elements is O(n) space. A recursive function adds a stack frame per call, so recursion depth of n is O(n) space even if it looks cheap. A two-dimensional table of size n by n, as in some dynamic programming, is O(n squared) space. There is often a **time-space trade-off**: for example, caching precomputed account balances in a map uses O(n) extra memory to turn repeated O(n) recomputation into O(1) lookups, which is exactly how we speed up hot banking queries.

A senior nuance is that Big-O hides constant factors that can matter in practice. An O(n log n) algorithm with a huge constant can be slower than an O(n squared) one for small n, and cache-friendliness and memory locality affect real speed beyond the Big-O class. Also, amortized complexity matters: adding to an `ArrayList` is amortized O(1) even though an occasional resize is O(n), because the expensive resizes are rare and spread out. So Big-O is the primary tool for reasoning about scale, but you still measure on real data for the final word.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's fraud team needs to find whether a specific account exists in today's transaction batch and, separately, whether any two transactions have the same reference id (a duplicate). A junior engineer wrote the duplicate check as a double loop comparing every transaction with every other, which worked fine on a test file of fifty rows but took minutes on the real file of a hundred thousand rows. This is a complexity problem — the double loop is O(n squared), and we need to understand why and how to fix it.

Problem 2 — We want to demonstrate the difference concretely by implementing the same two tasks at different complexities: a linear scan versus a constant-time map lookup for existence, and an O(n squared) nested-loop duplicate check versus an O(n) set-based check. We will count the operations so the reader literally sees the growth difference.

In the mini-project we will build a small `TransactionAnalyzer` that offers several methods: an O(n) linear search for an account, an O(1) map lookup for the same, an O(n squared) duplicate detector, and an O(n) set-based duplicate detector. We will run them on a batch and print the operation counts so the Big-O behaviour is visible. The data uses Rajesh and Priya's transactions.

The code contains: a `Transaction` model; a `TransactionAnalyzer` with the four methods and operation counters; and a `main` that runs them and prints counts.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a batch of one thousand transactions plus one deliberate duplicate reference id, TXN-500.

Step 1: We build the batch. `linearContains` searches for TXN-750 by walking the list from the start. It checks seven hundred fifty elements before finding it, so the operation count is 750. For a list of size n, the worst case is n checks, which is O(n). Doubling the batch doubles the work.

Step 2: `mapContains` first builds a `HashMap` keyed by reference id, which costs one pass of n inserts. After that, checking whether TXN-750 exists is a single hash lookup, which is O(1) regardless of batch size. This is the time-space trade-off: we spent O(n) extra memory on the map to make each future lookup constant time.

Step 3: `hasDuplicateNaive` compares every pair of transactions. For the first element it compares with all the rest, for the second with all after it, and so on. With about a thousand elements this is roughly half a million comparisons, which is O(n squared). On a hundred thousand rows it would be about five billion comparisons, which is why it took minutes in production.

Step 4: `hasDuplicateSet` makes a single pass, adding each reference id to a `HashSet`. `add` returns false if the id is already present, instantly revealing the duplicate. This is one pass of n, so O(n) time with O(n) extra space for the set. It finds the duplicate as soon as it reaches the repeated TXN-500.

Step 5: The operation counts printed make the growth concrete: the set-based check uses far fewer operations than the naive one, and the gap widens dramatically as n grows.

```
2026-10-26 10:20:00 [INFO] === Existence check ===
2026-10-26 10:20:00 [INFO] linearContains O(n): found after 750 ops
2026-10-26 10:20:00 [INFO] mapContains O(1) lookup: found=true (map built in O(n) once)
2026-10-26 10:20:00 [INFO] === Duplicate detection ===
2026-10-26 10:20:00 [WARNING] hasDuplicateNaive O(n^2): duplicate found after 499500 ops
2026-10-26 10:20:00 [WARNING] hasDuplicateSet O(n): duplicate found after 501 ops
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  batch size n = 1001 (one duplicate: TXN-500)
    │
    ├─ linearContains(TXN-750) ── walk list ──→ 750 ops          O(n)
    │
    ├─ mapContains(TXN-750) ── build map (n) ─→ 1 lookup         O(1) lookup / O(n) space
    │
    ├─ hasDuplicateNaive ── nested loop ──────→ 499,500 ops      O(n^2)
    │
    └─ hasDuplicateSet ── one pass + HashSet ─→ 501 ops          O(n)  / O(n) space

  Growth as n doubles:
    O(1)     : same
    O(log n) : +1 step
    O(n)     : ×2
    O(n log n): ×~2.1
    O(n^2)   : ×4   ← why the naive check exploded in production
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Time complexity describes how an algorithm's running time grows as the input grows, and space complexity describes how its extra memory grows. Both are expressed in Big-O notation, which captures the dominant growth rate and ignores constant factors and lower-order terms, so I can compare algorithms independently of hardware and predict behaviour as data scales from thousands to millions of rows.

The common classes I always rattle off with banking examples are these. Constant time, O(1), is a HashMap lookup of an account by id — it does not matter how many customers exist. Logarithmic, O(log n), is binary search on a sorted ledger or a TreeMap lookup, growing by only one step each time the data doubles. Linear, O(n), is summing every transaction once. O(n log n) is sorting the day's transactions. Quadratic, O(n squared), is a naive double loop comparing every transaction with every other, and exponential or factorial appear in brute-force combinatorial problems that are impractical beyond tiny inputs.

I like to tell a concrete story from my banking project. Our fraud duplicate-check was written as a nested double loop, which is O(n squared). It ran fine on a fifty-row test file but took minutes on the real hundred-thousand-row file, because a hundred thousand squared is ten billion comparisons. I rewrote it as a single pass using a HashSet, which is O(n) time with O(n) extra memory, and it finished in a fraction of a second. That is the practical payoff of understanding complexity.

Space complexity follows the same logic but counts memory, usually excluding the input, and recursion counts because each call adds a stack frame. The important idea I always mention is the time-space trade-off: caching precomputed balances in a map spends O(n) extra memory to turn repeated O(n) recomputation into O(1) lookups, which is exactly how we speed up hot banking queries. Finally, I note that Big-O hides constant factors and cache effects, and that some operations like ArrayList add are amortized O(1), so Big-O is my primary tool for reasoning about scale, but I still measure on real data for the final word.

keyPoints: DRY: Do not Repeat Yourself — extract common logic
KISS: Keep It Simple — simplest solution that works
YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It — do not build for imagined futures
Balance: DRY vs readability, YAGNI vs preparedness
